# Project conventions

winterm-browser is a Windows-native port. Its conventions are inherited from two places, and where
they disagree with general taste, they win.

## From upstream terminal-browser, which is being vendored

- Rust: `cargo nextest run --workspace`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`,
  `cargo fmt --all --check`. Warnings are errors.
- `pixel-core` lints deny undocumented unsafe blocks and warn on `unsafe_code` crate-wide. A port
  that reaches for Win32 will need unsafe; it must be documented to build.
- TypeScript packages test with `node --test`.
- 37 upstream Rust source files carry tests. They are the regression net for the modules this port
  claims not to touch.

## From agwinterm, the host terminal, whose plan is under triage alongside this one

- The control API is a versioned contract. `tests/conformance/control-api.json` is shared with a
  second product (agliteterm) and running in both repositories' CI, so a verb added there breaks a
  project that does not implement it.
- Never test against the real running instance or its data dir. A Debug build gets instance id
  `agwinterm-dev` with its own pipe and data dir; routing must be verified before results are
  trusted. Running against the real data dir has destroyed real user session state before.
- MSBuild silently serves stale DLLs in several documented ways. "It builds" is not evidence the
  new code ran.

## How this project is built

ralphex executes plans autonomously, task by task. revmux reviews every plan and every diff before
it is accepted. `.revmux/` is committed, so the review standard is versioned with the code.

A checked-in lens is executed by a headless agent with a shell. Treat `.revmux/` as code.

1	# winterm-browser — port brief
2	
3	A Windows-native port of [zenbu-labs/terminal-browser](https://github.com/zenbu-labs/terminal-browser):
4	a real Chromium browser rendered inside a terminal pane. The host terminal is
5	[agwinterm](file:///C:/Users/boris/source/agwinterm) (`TERM_PROGRAM=agwinterm`).
6	
7	Upstream sources are kept for reference (never committed) at `.reference/terminal-browser/`.
8	The agwinterm source tree lives at `C:\Users\boris\source\agwinterm`.
9	
10	## Why a port and not a build flag
11	
12	Upstream cannot run on Windows, for two *independent* reasons. Either alone is fatal.
13	
14	### Blocker 1 — the Rust engine does not compile on Windows
15	
16	`cargo check --workspace` in `.reference/terminal-browser/engine/` on `windows/amd64`,
17	Rust 1.93.1 (the pinned `rust-toolchain.toml` channel), fails with **41 errors** in `pixel-core`.
18	The unix assumptions are unconditional — not `cfg`-gated — so there is nothing to switch on:
19	
20	| upstream file | unix-only API |
21	|---|---|
22	| `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/terminal.rs:4` | `rustix::termios::{OptionalActions, Termios}` — raw mode via `tcgetattr`/`tcsetattr` |
23	| `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/terminal.rs:505,544` | `rustix::shm::unlink` |
24	| `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/terminal.rs:1161` | `OpenOptions::mode(0o600)` (unix-only trait) |
25	| `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/terminal.rs:770` | `rustix::pipe::pipe` + `fcntl_setfl(O_NONBLOCK)` |
26	| `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/herdr.rs:2,308` | `std::os::unix::net::{UnixStream, UnixListener}` |
27	| `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/ghostty.rs:121` | `rustix::process::kill_process(pid, Signal::USR2)` |
28	
29	`pixel-node` gates its zero-copy surface transports on `cfg(target_os="macos")` (IOSurface) and
30	`cfg(target_os="linux")` (shm). **There is no `cfg(windows)` anywhere in the workspace.**
31	The installer agrees: `scripts/install.sh:9-14` maps only `Darwin-arm64`, `Linux-x86_64`,
32	`Linux-aarch64`, and otherwise prints *"terminal-browser does not support …"*.
33	
34	### Blocker 2 — ConPTY strips the transport
35	
36	Upstream's entire output model is *write Kitty graphics APC escapes to stdout at frame rate*.
37	On Windows, ConPTY strips APC before the host emulator ever sees it. agwinterm's own gap
38	analysis states this (`docs/agterm-gap-analysis.md:41`):
39	
40	> Kitty graphics via the control pipe (docxy), delivered out-of-band because ConPTY strips APC.
41	
42	So even a hypothetical compiling `pixel-core` would paint a blank pane. The transport must change,
43	which is the real reason this is a port rather than a patch.
44	
45	## What agwinterm already gives us
46	
47	The host side is further along than the guest side, and this is what makes the port tractable:
48	
49	- **Kitty graphics model** — `Agwinterm.Core/KittyGraphics.cs` holds `KittyImage` (raw PNG or
50	  RGB/RGBA pixels) and `ImagePlacement` with `Cols`/`Rows` cell-span scaling (Kitty `c=`/`r=`),
51	  so one full-pane image scales to the grid. Parsing lives in
52	  `native/agwinterm-core/src/emulator.rs` (`finalize_kitty_image`, `parse_kitty_keys`).
53	- **An out-of-band frame path already exists** — `Agwinterm.Pty/ControlServer.cs:249`
54	  `image.frame` takes an `images[]` array, content-signature-caches each id to skip
55	  re-transmits, reads pixel bytes *off* the render lock, and swaps placements under a
56	  microsecond-scale lock. It is a video path fed by file paths.
57	- **Input is solved** — SGR mouse (`?1000/?1002/?1003/?1006`,
58	  `Agwinterm.Core/TerminalEmulator.cs:403-405`) and the kitty keyboard protocol
59	  (`emulator.rs:809 kitty_keyboard`). No macOS-style background helper app is needed;
60	  upstream's Swift input helper has no analogue here and is simply dropped.
61	
62	## Architecture
63	
64	An earlier draft of this brief proposed dropping `pixel-core` wholesale and letting agwinterm
65	composite. Measurement says otherwise, and the cheaper design won.
66	
67	### The unix dependency is concentrated, not pervasive
68	
69	Counting `rustix::` / `std::os::unix` / `termios` / `libc::` / `/dev/tty` references per module
70	across `pixel-core`'s 22 source files:
71	
72	| module | hits | disposition |
73	|---|---|---|
74	| `terminal.rs` | **64** | replace — this is the tty layer and the Kitty-to-stdout encoder |
75	| `herdr.rs` | 2 | port — `UnixStream`/`UnixListener` → Windows named pipes (or gate off for v1) |
76	| `ghostty.rs` | 2 | drop — ghostty-specific `SIGUSR2` signalling, no Windows analogue |
77	| **all 19 others** | **0** | **keep unchanged** |
78	
79	`canvas.rs`, `paint.rs`, `text_input.rs`, `image_cache.rs`, `menu.rs`, `kitty.rs`, `shape.rs`,
80	`wrap.rs`, `style.rs`, `scrollbar.rs` and the rest are already portable Rust — taffy, tiny-skia and
81	fontdue are all cross-platform. **The compositor and UI toolkit port for free.** This matters
82	because the browser chrome (tab strip, URL bar, menus, modals — `browser/src/ui/*.tsx`) renders
83	through `pixel-react` into `pixel-core`. Dropping `pixel-core` would have meant rewriting the entire
84	browser chrome; keeping it means the chrome is untouched.
85	
86	So the port is: **replace one module, port one, drop one, keep nineteen.**
87	
88	### No patched Electron needed
89	
90	Upstream's fast paths require an Electron fork they build themselves
91	(`scripts/fetch-electron.sh` pulls from `zenbu-labs/electron-releases`, macOS and Linux only) —
92	`useSharedTexture` on darwin, `useSharedMemory` on linux (`browser/src/page/offscreen.ts`).
93	
94	But `presentPaint` already falls through to `presentBitmap` (`browser/src/page/paint.ts:104`),
95	which uses stock Electron's `paint` event: `image.toBitmap()` →
96	`surface.present({ bgra, width, height, damage })`, coalesced by `BitmapPresenter`. That path
97	runs on **stock Electron on Windows with no patch**, and `Surface.present` is the exact seam the
98	Windows backend plugs into.
99	
100	Optimising past the bitmap copy is deliberately deferred. Stock Electron on Windows can expose a
101	D3D11 shared-texture handle, and agwinterm renders with Direct2D, so a genuine zero-copy path
102	exists later — it is not v1.
103	
104	| layer | upstream (macOS/Linux) | winterm-browser |
105	|---|---|---|
106	| Browser + chrome UI | Electron OSR + React via `pixel-react` | **unchanged** |
107	| Compositor / layout / text | `pixel-core` (taffy / tiny-skia / fontdue) | **unchanged** — already portable |
108	| Electron frame capture | patched Electron: IOSurface / shm | **stock Electron bitmap path** (already written) |
109	| Frame pixels → terminal | Kitty APC → stdout | Windows file-mapping shared BGRA ring → control pipe |
110	| tty layer (`terminal.rs`) | termios raw mode, `/dev/tty`, shm, kitty encoder | **rewritten** for Windows console + agwinterm |
111	| Raw-mode input | termios + macOS Swift helper | Windows console VT input; helper dropped entirely |
112	| `herdr.rs` IPC | `UnixStream` | Windows named pipes |
113	| `ghostty.rs` | `SIGUSR2` to ghostty | dropped |
114	| CLI / terminals / store | TypeScript | mostly portable; `ssh.ts` and `sandbox.ts` (apparmor) need Windows work |
115	
116	### Chosen transport
117	
118	Extend agwinterm with a shared-memory frame command so Electron's paint buffer reaches the
119	renderer with **no PNG encode, no disk round-trip and no base64**:
120	
121	```
122	Electron paint(BGRA)
123	  └─> CreateFileMapping (shared BGRA ring)
124	        └─> pipe: {"cmd":"image.frameshm","args":{"handle":..,"w":..,"h":..}}
125	              └─> KittyImage (f=32, raw RGBA)
126	                    └─> D2D texture
127	```
128	
129	This spans **two repositories**: agwinterm gains the command, winterm-browser produces the frames.
130	The existing file-based `image.frame` stays as the fallback and as the bring-up path.
131	
132	## Working agreement
133	
134	- **ralphex** is the implementer. Plans live in `docs/plans/`; execution is autonomous.
135	- **revmux** is the review harness, run natively on Windows. Every plan and every diff goes

# winterm-browser — port brief

A Windows-native port of [zenbu-labs/terminal-browser](https://github.com/zenbu-labs/terminal-browser):
a real Chromium browser rendered inside a terminal pane. The host terminal is
[agwinterm](file:///C:/Users/boris/source/agwinterm) (`TERM_PROGRAM=agwinterm`).

Upstream sources are kept for reference (never committed) at `.reference/terminal-browser/`.
The agwinterm source tree lives at `C:\Users\boris\source\agwinterm`.

## Why a port and not a build flag

Upstream cannot run on Windows, for two *independent* reasons. Either alone is fatal.

### Blocker 1 — the Rust engine does not compile on Windows

`cargo check --workspace` in `.reference/terminal-browser/engine/` on `windows/amd64`,
Rust 1.93.1 (the pinned `rust-toolchain.toml` channel), fails with **41 errors** in `pixel-core`.
The unix assumptions are unconditional — not `cfg`-gated — so there is nothing to switch on:

| upstream file | unix-only API |
|---|---|
| `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/terminal.rs:4` | `rustix::termios::{OptionalActions, Termios}` — raw mode via `tcgetattr`/`tcsetattr` |
| `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/terminal.rs:505,544` | `rustix::shm::unlink` |
| `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/terminal.rs:1161` | `OpenOptions::mode(0o600)` (unix-only trait) |
| `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/terminal.rs:770` | `rustix::pipe::pipe` + `fcntl_setfl(O_NONBLOCK)` |
| `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/herdr.rs:2,308` | `std::os::unix::net::{UnixStream, UnixListener}` |
| `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/ghostty.rs:121` | `rustix::process::kill_process(pid, Signal::USR2)` |

`pixel-node` gates its zero-copy surface transports on `cfg(target_os="macos")` (IOSurface) and
`cfg(target_os="linux")` (shm). **There is no `cfg(windows)` anywhere in the workspace.**
The installer agrees: `scripts/install.sh:9-14` maps only `Darwin-arm64`, `Linux-x86_64`,
`Linux-aarch64`, and otherwise prints *"terminal-browser does not support …"*.

### Blocker 2 — ConPTY strips the transport

Upstream's entire output model is *write Kitty graphics APC escapes to stdout at frame rate*.
On Windows, ConPTY strips APC before the host emulator ever sees it. agwinterm's own gap
analysis states this (`docs/agterm-gap-analysis.md:41`):

> Kitty graphics via the control pipe (docxy), delivered out-of-band because ConPTY strips APC.

So even a hypothetical compiling `pixel-core` would paint a blank pane. The transport must change,
which is the real reason this is a port rather than a patch.

## What agwinterm already gives us

The host side is further along than the guest side, and this is what makes the port tractable:

- **Kitty graphics model** — `Agwinterm.Core/KittyGraphics.cs` holds `KittyImage` (raw PNG or
  RGB/RGBA pixels) and `ImagePlacement` with `Cols`/`Rows` cell-span scaling (Kitty `c=`/`r=`),
  so one full-pane image scales to the grid. Parsing lives in
  `native/agwinterm-core/src/emulator.rs` (`finalize_kitty_image`, `parse_kitty_keys`).
- **An out-of-band frame path already exists** — `Agwinterm.Pty/ControlServer.cs:249`
  `image.frame` takes an `images[]` array, content-signature-caches each id to skip
  re-transmits, reads pixel bytes *off* the render lock, and swaps placements under a
  microsecond-scale lock. It is a video path fed by file paths.
- **Input is solved** — SGR mouse (`?1000/?1002/?1003/?1006`,
  `Agwinterm.Core/TerminalEmulator.cs:403-405`) and the kitty keyboard protocol
  (`emulator.rs:809 kitty_keyboard`). No macOS-style background helper app is needed;
  upstream's Swift input helper has no analogue here and is simply dropped.

## Architecture

An earlier draft of this brief proposed dropping `pixel-core` wholesale and letting agwinterm
composite. Measurement says otherwise, and the cheaper design won.

### The unix dependency is concentrated, not pervasive

Counting `rustix::` / `std::os::unix` / `termios` / `libc::` / `/dev/tty` references per module
across `pixel-core`'s 22 source files:

| module | hits | disposition |
|---|---|---|
| `terminal.rs` | **64** | replace — this is the tty layer and the Kitty-to-stdout encoder |
| `herdr.rs` | 2 | port — `UnixStream`/`UnixListener` → Windows named pipes (or gate off for v1) |
| `ghostty.rs` | 2 | drop — ghostty-specific `SIGUSR2` signalling, no Windows analogue |
| **all 19 others** | **0** | **keep unchanged** |

`canvas.rs`, `paint.rs`, `text_input.rs`, `image_cache.rs`, `menu.rs`, `kitty.rs`, `shape.rs`,
`wrap.rs`, `style.rs`, `scrollbar.rs` and the rest are already portable Rust — taffy, tiny-skia and
fontdue are all cross-platform. **The compositor and UI toolkit port for free.** This matters
because the browser chrome (tab strip, URL bar, menus, modals — `browser/src/ui/*.tsx`) renders
through `pixel-react` into `pixel-core`. Dropping `pixel-core` would have meant rewriting the entire
browser chrome; keeping it means the chrome is untouched.

So the port is: **replace one module, port one, drop one, keep nineteen.**

### No patched Electron needed

Upstream's fast paths require an Electron fork they build themselves
(`scripts/fetch-electron.sh` pulls from `zenbu-labs/electron-releases`, macOS and Linux only) —
`useSharedTexture` on darwin, `useSharedMemory` on linux (`browser/src/page/offscreen.ts`).

But `presentPaint` already falls through to `presentBitmap` (`browser/src/page/paint.ts:104`),
which uses stock Electron's `paint` event: `image.toBitmap()` →
`surface.present({ bgra, width, height, damage })`, coalesced by `BitmapPresenter`. That path
runs on **stock Electron on Windows with no patch**, and `Surface.present` is the exact seam the
Windows backend plugs into.

Optimising past the bitmap copy is deliberately deferred. Stock Electron on Windows can expose a
D3D11 shared-texture handle, and agwinterm renders with Direct2D, so a genuine zero-copy path
exists later — it is not v1.

| layer | upstream (macOS/Linux) | winterm-browser |
|---|---|---|
| Browser + chrome UI | Electron OSR + React via `pixel-react` | **unchanged** |
| Compositor / layout / text | `pixel-core` (taffy / tiny-skia / fontdue) | **unchanged** — already portable |
| Electron frame capture | patched Electron: IOSurface / shm | **stock Electron bitmap path** (already written) |
| Frame pixels → terminal | Kitty APC → stdout | Windows file-mapping shared BGRA ring → control pipe |
| tty layer (`terminal.rs`) | termios raw mode, `/dev/tty`, shm, kitty encoder | **rewritten** for Windows console + agwinterm |
| Raw-mode input | termios + macOS Swift helper | Windows console VT input; helper dropped entirely |
| `herdr.rs` IPC | `UnixStream` | Windows named pipes |
| `ghostty.rs` | `SIGUSR2` to ghostty | dropped |
| CLI / terminals / store | TypeScript | mostly portable; `ssh.ts` and `sandbox.ts` (apparmor) need Windows work |

### Chosen transport

Extend agwinterm with a shared-memory frame command so Electron's paint buffer reaches the
renderer with **no PNG encode, no disk round-trip and no base64**:

```
Electron paint(BGRA)
  └─> CreateFileMapping (shared BGRA ring)
        └─> pipe: {"cmd":"image.frameshm","args":{"handle":..,"w":..,"h":..}}
              └─> KittyImage (f=32, raw RGBA)
                    └─> D2D texture
```

This spans **two repositories**: agwinterm gains the command, winterm-browser produces the frames.
The existing file-based `image.frame` stays as the fallback and as the bring-up path.

## Working agreement

- **ralphex** is the implementer. Plans live in `docs/plans/`; execution is autonomous.
- **revmux** is the review harness, run natively on Windows. Every plan and every diff goes
  through it before it is accepted. `.revmux/` is committed, so the review standard is versioned
  with the code.
- Both `claude` and `codex` CLIs are present, so full-roster profiles (`comprehensive`,
  `grill-me`) are available rather than `claude-only`.

## Verified environment

Established by direct check on this machine, 2026-08-21:

| tool | state |
|---|---|
| Windows | 11 Home Single Language, 10.0.26200 |
| agwinterm | 0.17.2, `AGWINTERM_ENABLED=1` |
| Go | 1.26.1 windows/amd64 |
| Rust | cargo 1.96.0 |
| Node | v22.19.0 |
| Python | 3.13.7 |
| revmux | builds and runs natively on Windows (`lock_windows.go`, `procgroup_windows.go`); both `--task` and `/task:` flag styles accepted |
| ralphex | installed at `~/go/bin/ralphex.exe` |
| claude / codex | both on PATH |
| WSL | **not installed — and explicitly out of scope.** This is a Windows-native port. |

# winterm-browser — Windows-native port

## Overview

Bring terminal-browser to Windows, hosted by agwinterm: a real Chromium browser rendered inside a
terminal pane, with working keyboard and mouse, on stock Electron, with no WSL.

The authoritative design is [`docs/design/00-port-brief.md`](../design/00-port-brief.md). Read it
first — it records what was measured rather than assumed, and it already overturned one plausible
architecture. In short:

- Upstream cannot run here for two independent reasons: `pixel-core` does not compile on Windows
  (41 errors), and its transport — Kitty APC escapes on stdout — is stripped by ConPTY before any
  Windows emulator sees it.
- But the unix dependency is **concentrated, not pervasive**: 64 of 68 unix-API references live in
  `terminal.rs`, and **19 of 22 `pixel-core` modules have none at all**. The compositor, layout and
  text stack (taffy, tiny-skia, fontdue) are portable Rust. That matters because the browser chrome
  renders through `pixel-react` into `pixel-core` — dropping it would have meant rewriting the whole
  chrome.
- Upstream's fast frame paths need an Electron fork they build themselves, macOS and Linux only. But
  `presentBitmap` (`browser/src/page/paint.ts:104`) already implements a stock-Electron path:
  `image.toBitmap()` → `surface.present({bgra, width, height, damage})`. Windows gets that for free.

**So the port is: replace one module, port one, drop one, keep nineteen** — plus a new output
backend that speaks agwinterm's control pipe instead of writing escapes to a tty.

## Context (from discovery)

Upstream reference (read-only, never committed): `.reference/terminal-browser/`.
agwinterm source: `C:\Users\boris\source\agwinterm`.

| area | file | note |
|---|---|---|
| tty layer to replace | `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/terminal.rs` | 64 unix hits: termios raw mode, `/dev/tty`, `rustix::shm`, `pipe`+`O_NONBLOCK`, and the Kitty-to-stdout encoder |
| IPC to port | `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/herdr.rs` | `UnixStream`/`UnixListener` → named pipes, or gated off for v1 |
| to drop | `engine/crates/pixel-core/src/ghostty.rs` | `SIGUSR2` to ghostty; no Windows analogue |
| keep unchanged | the other 19 `pixel-core` modules | `canvas`, `paint`, `text_input`, `image_cache`, `menu`, `kitty`, `shape`, `wrap`, `style`, `scrollbar`, … |
| napi bridge | `engine/crates/pixel-node/src/{lib,surface}.rs` | `SurfacePixels` gates IOSurface on macOS and shm on linux; the `Owned { bgra, width, height }` variant is the Windows path and already exists |
| the seam | `Surface.present` from `pixel-react` | what `browser/` calls; the Windows backend plugs in here |
| Electron capture | `browser/src/page/{offscreen,paint}.ts` | `offscreenPreferences` branches darwin/linux; `initOffscreenMode` throws on darwin without shared textures |
| host frame path | agwinterm `src/Agwinterm.Pty/ControlServer.cs:249` | `image.frame` today; `image.frameshm` per the agwinterm plan |
| host input | agwinterm `TerminalEmulator.cs:403-405`, `emulator.rs:809` | SGR mouse `?1000/?1002/?1003/?1006` and kitty keyboard already work |

**Tooling upstream already uses**, and this port keeps: `cargo nextest run --workspace`,
`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --all --check`, and
`node --test` for the TypeScript packages. 37 Rust source files carry tests; they are the
regression net for everything in the "keep unchanged" column.

## Constraints

- **Windows-native only. WSL is out of scope** and is not an acceptable fallback for any task.
- **Stock Electron.** Do not fetch or build a patched Electron; if a task seems to need one, the
  task is wrong. `scripts/fetch-electron.sh` is upstream's, and it does not apply here.
- **This plan depends on the agwinterm plan** for the shm fast path only
  (`agwinterm/docs/plans/20260821-image-frameshm-command.md`, contract in
  `agwinterm/docs/specs/image-frameshm.md`). Everything up to and including the
  first-frame-on-screen milestone uses the file-based `image.frame`, which needs no agwinterm change.
  If the contract is not ready when Task 9 starts, stop and say so rather than inventing a shape.
- **Never test against the real agwinterm instance.** Use a Debug agwinterm (instance id
  `agwinterm-dev`, its own pipe and data dir) and verify routing with
  `agwintermctl --pipe agwinterm-dev tree` before trusting any result. Running against the real
  data dir has destroyed real session state before.
- **Do not weaken the "keep unchanged" 19 modules to make something compile.** If one of them needs
  a change, that is a finding worth recording in the plan (➕), not a quiet edit.
- Upstream's licence and provenance travel with the vendored code.

## Development Approach

- **Testing approach**: Regular (code first, then tests).
- Complete each task fully before moving to the next.
- Make small, focused changes.
- **CRITICAL: every task MUST include new/updated tests** for code changes in that task.
  - unit tests for new and modified functions, as separate checklist items
  - success and error scenarios both
- **CRITICAL: all tests must pass before starting the next task.**
- **CRITICAL: update this plan file when scope changes during implementation.**
- Run `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` as part of "tests pass".

## Testing Strategy

- **Unit tests**: required every task. Rust via `cargo nextest`, TypeScript via `node --test`.
- **Platform-behaviour tests**: the console and control-pipe layers are where assumptions die.
  Prefer a test that drives the real thing (a real named pipe, a real `MemoryMappedFile`, a real
  Debug agwinterm) over a mock that encodes a guess about Win32.
- **Visual confirmation** is a milestone, not a test: Task 8 is "a page is legibly on screen".
  Screenshot verification belongs in Post-Completion, not in a checkbox.
- **No e2e browser-automation suite in this plan.** Scope is a working port.

## Progress Tracking

- Mark completed items with `[x]` immediately when done.
- Add newly discovered tasks with ➕ prefix.
- Document issues/blockers with ⚠️ prefix.
- Update the plan when implementation deviates from scope.

## Implementation Steps

### Task 1: Vendor upstream and record the true Windows baseline

- [ ] copy upstream `engine/`, `browser/`, `cli/`, `terminals/`, `store/` from `.reference/` into the
      repo root, preserving `LICENSE` and recording the upstream commit in `docs/design/UPSTREAM.md`
- [ ] do **not** copy `scripts/` wholesale — `install.sh`, `fetch-electron.sh`, `apparmor.sh` and
      `bundle.sh` are unix/patched-Electron specific; port them later, individually, when needed
- [ ] run `cargo check --workspace` and commit the full error list to
      `docs/design/01-baseline-errors.md`, grouped by module

      frame, and wake the event loop

      the seam upstream already implies, so the 19 portable modules keep compiling untouched
- [ ] move the existing unix implementation behind `#[cfg(unix)]` so upstream behaviour is preserved

- [ ] add a `#[cfg(windows)]` stub that compiles and returns "unimplemented" for every method
- [ ] `#[cfg(unix)]`-gate `ghostty.rs` and `herdr.rs` for now, recording herdr as deferred
- [ ] write tests that the trait's contract holds for a fake backend (event delivery ordering,

      keyboard forms, SGR press/drag/release, and a sequence split across two reads
- [ ] write tests for raw-mode restoration on both the normal and panicking exit path

### Task 4: agwinterm control-pipe client

- [ ] implement a Rust client for the agwinterm control pipe: connect to the pipe named by

      `{"ok":true,"result":...}` / `{"ok":false,"error":...}` envelope back
- [ ] target the session named by `%AGWINTERM_SESSION_ID%` rather than `"active"`, so a frame can
      never land in a pane the user switched to

      instead of producing a blank pane
- [ ] handle a closed or unavailable pipe as a recoverable error with reconnect, not a panic
- [ ] write tests against a real named-pipe server fixture: request/response round-trip, an error
      envelope, a server that closes mid-request, and a server that never accepts
- [ ] write tests for host detection with the env vars present and absent
- [ ] run tests — must pass before Task 5

### Task 5: File-based frame output (bring-up path)

- [ ] implement the output half of the Windows backend using the **existing** `image.frame` command:
      encode the composited frame to PNG, write it to a temp path, and publish it via the control
      pipe with `cols`/`rows` set to the pane's cell span so it scales to the grid
- [ ] reuse ids across frames so agwinterm's content-signature cache behaves as designed
- [ ] clean up temp files, and survive a frame whose file write fails
- [ ] keep this path permanently as the fallback and as the thing the shm path is diffed against —
      it is not throwaway scaffolding
- [ ] write tests for cell-span computation from pixel size and cell metrics, including a pane too
      small to place into
- [ ] write tests for the publish path against the named-pipe fixture from Task 4
- [ ] run tests — must pass before Task 6

### Task 6: `pixel-node` on Windows

- [ ] make `pixel-node` build on Windows: the `Owned { bgra, width, height }` variant of
      `SurfacePixels` already exists and is the Windows path
- [ ] give `draw_frame`'s match a Windows-valid arm set, and confirm `surface.rs` has no

- [ ] confirm the napi module loads under Node v22 on Windows

- [ ] run tests — must pass before Task 7

- [ ] add a Windows branch to `offscreenPreferences` in `browser/src/page/offscreen.ts` returning
      `{ useSharedTexture: false, deviceScaleFactor }` — no shared memory, no patched build
- [ ] make `initOffscreenMode` report `bitmap` on Windows without throwing
- [ ] confirm `presentPaint` falls through to `presentBitmap` and that `BitmapPresenter`'s coalescing

- [ ] write tests for `offscreenPreferences` per platform
- [ ] write tests for `presentPaint` selecting the bitmap path when no texture and no shm frame are

      file-based path, into a Debug agwinterm pane
- [ ] load a static page and confirm it is legibly on screen at the right size and position

1	# Shared-memory frame command (`image.frameshm`)
2	
3	## Overview
4	
5	Add a control-pipe command that accepts browser-rate BGRA frames through a shared memory mapping
6	instead of through files, so a producer can drive a pane at video rates without a PNG encode or a
7	disk round-trip on every frame.
8	
9	The consumer is [winterm-browser](file:///C:/Users/boris/source/winterm-browser), a Windows-native
10	port of terminal-browser that renders Chromium into an agwinterm pane. Its design brief is
11	`C:\Users\boris\source\winterm-browser\docs\design\00-port-brief.md`. That project is blocked on
12	this command, and this plan defines the contract it codes against — so the wire shape here is the
13	deliverable, not just the implementation.
14	
15	**Problem it solves.** `image.frame` (`ControlServer.cs:249`) is already a frame path: it takes an
16	`images[]` array, content-signature-caches each id to skip re-transmits, reads pixel bytes off the
17	render lock, and swaps placements under a microsecond-scale lock. But every image arrives as a
18	`path`, so a 30fps full-pane producer must PNG-encode and write a file 30 times a second and
19	agwinterm must read it back. For a document viewer like docxy that is fine. For a browser it is not.
20	
21	**Why this is worth doing beyond the browser.** The expensive part of `image.frame` is not the
22	placement machinery, which is already good — it is the format and the transport. Anything that
23	generates pixels rather than loading them (a video preview, a plot that animates, a remote frame
24	buffer) hits the same wall.
25	
26	## Context (from discovery)
27	
28	- `src/Agwinterm.Pty/ControlServer.cs:249` — `image.frame` dispatch; `HandleImageFrame` at ~line 425
29	  is the model to follow: phase 1 resolves placements and owns pixel bytes **off** the render lock,
30	  phase 2 takes a brief lock for dictionary/list swaps only.
31	- `src/Agwinterm.Core/KittyGraphics.cs` — `KittyFormat { Rgb = 24, Rgba = 32, Png = 100 }`,
32	  `KittyImage(Id, Format, Width, Height, Data)`, `ImagePlacement(ImageId, Row, Col, Cols, Rows,
33	  SrcX, SrcY, SrcW, SrcH)`.
34	- `src/Agwinterm.Pty/ISession.cs:64,66` — `Inject(ReadOnlySpan<byte>)` and
35	  `MutateLocked(Action<ITerminalCore>)`; both take the render lock internally.
36	- `tests/Agwinterm.Pty.Tests/ControlServerTests.cs` and `ControlApiTests.cs` — where control-verb
37	  tests live.
38	- `tests/conformance/control-api.json` — **shared with agliteterm**; the same spec runs in both
39	  repositories' CI. See the constraint below.
40	
41	## Constraints
42	
43	- **Do not add `image.frameshm` to `tests/conformance/control-api.json`.** That file is a contract
44	  agliteterm must also satisfy, and adding a verb there fails agliteterm's build for a command it
45	  does not implement. Test this verb in agwinterm's own xunit suites only. If it should later become
46	  part of the shared dialect, that is a separate decision made with agliteterm in hand.
47	- **Frames must never tear.** A producer writing while the renderer reads is the default failure
48	  mode of any shared buffer; the design must make a torn read impossible, not unlikely.
49	- **A dead or lying producer must not take the terminal down.** The name, dimensions, stride and
50	  offsets all arrive from another process and every one of them is untrusted input into a pointer
51	  computation. Validate against the actual mapped view length before any copy.
52	- **`ControlServer` int args must be JSON numbers, not strings** — `GetInt` throws
53	  `"requires an element of type 'Number'"` otherwise. The ctl serializes `cargs` by type, so parse
54	  with `int.TryParse` on the CLI side.
55	- Backward compatibility: `image.frame` keeps working unchanged. This is an additional verb.
56	- Build discipline (these have cost hours before): close the running dev instance before building;
57	  build `src/Agwinterm.Win32` **explicitly** so its copy of `Agwinterm.Pty.dll` is not stale;
58	  a plain solution build outputs to a *different* directory than a project build.
59	- Test against an isolated instance: a Debug build auto-uses instance id `agwinterm-dev` with its own
60	  data dir and pipe. Drive it with `agwintermctl --pipe agwinterm-dev`. **Never** run against the
61	  real `agwinterm` pipe or data dir.

65	- **Testing approach**: Regular (code first, then tests).
66	- Complete each task fully before moving to the next.
67	- Make small, focused changes.

69	  - unit tests for new and modified methods, listed as separate checklist items
70	  - both success and error scenarios — for this plan the error scenarios are the point, since
71	    most of the risk is malformed input from another process
72	- **CRITICAL: all tests must pass before starting the next task.**
73	- **CRITICAL: update this plan file when scope changes during implementation.**

# Shared-memory frame command (`image.frameshm`)

## Overview

Add a control-pipe command that accepts browser-rate BGRA frames through a shared memory mapping
instead of through files, so a producer can drive a pane at video rates without a PNG encode or a
disk round-trip on every frame.

The consumer is [winterm-browser](file:///C:/Users/boris/source/winterm-browser), a Windows-native
port of terminal-browser that renders Chromium into an agwinterm pane. Its design brief is
`C:\Users\boris\source\winterm-browser\docs\design\00-port-brief.md`. That project is blocked on
this command, and this plan defines the contract it codes against — so the wire shape here is the
deliverable, not just the implementation.

**Problem it solves.** `image.frame` (`ControlServer.cs:249`) is already a frame path: it takes an
`images[]` array, content-signature-caches each id to skip re-transmits, reads pixel bytes off the
render lock, and swaps placements under a microsecond-scale lock. But every image arrives as a
`path`, so a 30fps full-pane producer must PNG-encode and write a file 30 times a second and
agwinterm must read it back. For a document viewer like docxy that is fine. For a browser it is not.

**Why this is worth doing beyond the browser.** The expensive part of `image.frame` is not the
placement machinery, which is already good — it is the format and the transport. Anything that
generates pixels rather than loading them (a video preview, a plot that animates, a remote frame
buffer) hits the same wall.

  phase 2 takes a brief lock for dictionary/list swaps only.

  SrcX, SrcY, SrcW, SrcH)`.

  repositories' CI. See the constraint below.

findings.title: The engine runs in a detached daemon that opens the client's tty by path — a mechanism with no Windows analogue, and no task addresses it
findings.body:
Upstream is a daemon/client split, and the daemon reaches the user's terminal by opening a *path*. I traced the whole chain: `cli/src/main.ts:119` `ownTtyPath()` shells out to the unix `tty` command and keeps the result only if it `startsWith("/dev/")`; `main.ts:301-303` refuses to run without it (`"not running on a tty"`); the path is sent over a unix socket to the daemon, which at `browser/src/daemon.ts:96-106` rejects any open without a `tty` and passes it into `createSession`; `browser/src/session/session.tsx:315` hands it to `createRoot({ tty: this.ctx.tty, ... })`; and `pixel-core/src/terminal.rs:348-349` does `File::options().read(true).write(true).open(tty_path)`. Meanwhile `main.ts:155` spawns the daemon `{ detached: true, stdio: "ignore" }` — it has no console of its own by construction.

On Windows there is no path that names another process's ConPTY. `CONIN$`/`CONOUT$` resolve to the *calling* process's own console, and a detached process has none. `AttachConsole(pid)` is the only handle-across-processes mechanism, it is one-console-per-process, and it attaches to a console the caller does not own.

This is established. What follows from it is that Task 3's design is placed in the wrong process: it says "read from the console input handle" and "enable VT input with `SetConsoleMode`", which assumes the engine owns the user's console. In upstream's architecture the engine is the daemon and never does. The output side is accidentally immune — frames leave out-of-band via the control pipe addressed by `AGWINTERM_SESSION_ID`, so it does not need the tty — which is likely why this never surfaced during design. Input has no such escape: nothing in the 13 tasks proposes forwarding stdin from the CLI client to the daemon, hosting the engine in the foreground process instead, or duplicating a console handle across the boundary. An autonomous executor reaching Task 3 has to invent one of those architectures with no brief to work from.

What would overturn this: evidence that the port intends to abandon the daemon model and run the engine in the foreground CLI process (`createRoot({tty: null})` is a supported shape — `session.tsx:313` has a `!this.ctx.tty` branch). If that is the intent it is a large architectural decision that appears nowhere in the brief or the plan, and it needs to be a task.
findings.fix: Add a task before Task 3 that decides where the engine process lives on Windows and how console input reaches it — foreground-hosted engine, or client-forwards-stdin-over-IPC. Task 3's console work cannot be specified until that is settled.

findings.title: Task 8 cannot launch the browser: the only launcher is the CLI, which Task 11 ports three tasks later
findings.body:
Task 8's first checkbox is "launch Electron OSR". There is exactly one launcher in the tree and it is unported at that point.

`browser/package.json:9` — `"start": "... && exec node ../cli/dist/main.js"`. The CLI is the entry point. `cli/src/main.ts:109` builds the launch command as `return { command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", line], cwd: browserDir };` — every browser launch goes through `/bin/sh`, which does not exist on Windows. Before that, `main.ts:65-68` sets `ELECTRON_DEV_BIN` to `["electron"]` for every non-darwin platform, and `main.ts:83-86` does `fs.existsSync` on it and calls `fail()` if missing — on Windows the artifact is `electron.exe`, so it fails there first. `main.ts:105-108` also wraps arguments in POSIX single-quote escaping and appends `2>>'...'` shell redirection.

That work is Task 11 ("port `cli/src/` entry points: `main.ts`, ..."). So Task 8 — the milestone the goal names as the most valuable thing to get right — sits three tasks before the code that makes it possible. This is established from the two files; what follows is that an autonomous executor at Task 8 either stalls or silently pulls Task 11's work forward, which makes Task 11's later "tests pass" gate meaningless because the code will already be there under a different task's name.

What would overturn this: if Task 8 is meant to bypass the CLI and invoke `electron.exe browser/dist/main.js` by hand as throwaway scaffolding. The plan does not say that, and it would still need the daemon-vs-foreground question above answered first.
findings.fix: Move the `main.ts` launch path (electron binary resolution, spawn without `/bin/sh`) out of Task 11 and into a task before Task 8, leaving Task 11 with the registry/paths/`ssh`/`sandbox`/`upgrade` surface it also covers.

findings.title: Nothing supplies cell pixel metrics on Windows — both of pixel-core's mechanisms are unavailable against agwinterm
findings.body:
Cell size in pixels is what Tasks 5, 8 and 9 all compute against (Task 5: "cell-span computation from pixel size and cell metrics"; Task 9: "the pane's cell metrics, since an off-by-one cell is a wrong click target"). `pixel-core` has exactly two ways to learn it, and on Windows+agwinterm neither works.

`terminal.rs:869-889` `cell_size()`: first `self.size()?.cell_size()`, where `size()` at `terminal.rs:847-855` is `termios::tcgetwinsize` reading `ws_xpixel`/`ws_ypixel`. Windows' `GetConsoleScreenBufferInfo` has no pixel fields — there is no equivalent to report. Second, it writes `b"\x1b[16t"` (`terminal.rs:880`) and waits 300ms for a reply, setting `cell_query_unsupported` on timeout.

agwinterm answers neither. I read its full CSI dispatch at `native/agwinterm-core/src/emulator.rs:964-1045`: the arms are `H f A B C D G d J K X m r L M @ P S T q`, and everything else — including `t` — falls to `HostAction::Unhandled`. There is no XTWINOPS. I also grepped `src/Agwinterm.Pty/ControlServer.cs` for `cell_width`/`CellWidth`/`cell_height`/`CellHeight` and found nothing, so the control pipe does not expose it either, even though agwinterm computes `_cellW`/`_cellH` internally (`src/Agwinterm.App/MainWindow.xaml.cs:225-226`).

Established: both mechanisms are absent. What follows is that `cell_size()` returns `None` on this target, and every pixel↔cell conversion in Tasks 5/8/9 has no input. Note upstream's own herdr fixture (`pixel-core/src/herdr.rs:260`) carries `cell_width_px`/`cell_height_px` in its info payload — upstream solves this by asking the *terminal* over a side channel, which is precisely the mechanism agwinterm's control API does not offer yet.

What would overturn this: an agwinterm control verb or environment variable carrying cell metrics that I failed to find. I searched only for those four identifier spellings in `ControlServer.cs`.
findings.fix: Either add a cell-metrics field to an agwinterm control response (a third repo-crossing contract, so it belongs in the agwinterm plan next to `image.frameshm`), or add `CSI 16 t` to agwinterm's CSI dispatch. Pin it before Task 5, not during it.

findings.title: Mouse input is permanently cell-quantized against agwinterm; the brief's "Input is solved" overstates what the host can deliver
findings.body:
The brief states "**Input is solved** — SGR mouse ... No macOS-style background helper app is needed". The host cannot deliver pointer position better than one cell, and `pixel-core` has an explicit capability flag for exactly this that will read false.

agwinterm's encoder, `src/Agwinterm.Win32/Program.Input.cs:442-453`, computes `int col = ...(pxX - ox) / cw` and `int row = ...(pxY - oy) / ch` and emits `\x1b[<{btn};{col+1};{row+1}M`. Cell integers only — the sub-cell pixel offset is discarded before the sequence is built.

`pixel-core` probes for better: `terminal.rs:361` requests `\x1b[?1016h` (SGR-pixel mouse) at startup, and `terminal.rs:945-948` `probe_mouse_pixels()` sends `\x1b[?1016$p` and waits 150ms for a DECRQM reply. agwinterm has no `1016` anywhere (`emulator.rs:621-623` handles 1002/1003/1006 only), and its DECRQM handler at `emulator.rs:768-774` answers *only* for mode 2026. So the probe times out and `mouse_pixels = false`.

That flag is load-bearing, not cosmetic: `engine/mod.rs:352` sets it from `term.reports_pixel_mouse()`, `engine/pointer.rs:61` gates `let located = self.pixel_mouse.then_some(point)` so hover/pairing get no position, and `engine/scroll.rs:192` gates `wants_cursor` on it.

Established: the encoder, the probe, and agwinterm's lack of 1016. What follows is that a real Chromium browser gets pointer resolution of roughly one cell — upstream's own fixture at `herdr.rs:260` uses 9x19 px cells — so small link targets, hover states, drag-select and scrollbar grabs all quantize. Task 9 does plan a "cell coordinates to page pixels" translation, so the plan encodes the right arithmetic; the objection is that the brief presents this as parity when it is a permanent fidelity ceiling on the headline feature ("a real Chromium browser ... with working keyboard and mouse").

What would overturn this: adding `?1016` support to agwinterm and a pixel-coordinate branch to `SendMouse`. That is a small, well-localized change on the host side — but it is a second agwinterm dependency the plan does not have, and it is not in the agwinterm plan.
findings.fix: Either add `?1016` + pixel coordinates to agwinterm's mouse encoder as a second item in the agwinterm plan, or state the cell-resolution ceiling in the brief so it reads as an accepted cost rather than an oversight.

findings.title: Task 1's `pnpm install` runs the patched-Electron fetch script the plan forbids, via bash
findings.body:
`browser/package.json:7` is `"postinstall": "bash ../scripts/fetch-electron.sh"`.

Task 1 says to run `pnpm install` and record what installs cleanly, and in the same task says "do **not** copy `scripts/` wholesale — `install.sh`, `fetch-electron.sh`, `apparmor.sh` and `bundle.sh` are unix/patched-Electron specific". Those two bullets are in direct conflict: with `scripts/` uncopied, `pnpm install` runs `bash` on a file that is not there; with it copied, it runs the script the Constraints section forbids ("Do not fetch or build a patched Electron"). Either way `pnpm install` fails or does the wrong thing, in the very first task, and the plan presents its outcome as a recording exercise rather than a thing that needs fixing.

This also makes Task 7's premise slightly optimistic. Task 7 correctly identifies `presentBitmap` as a stock-Electron path, but the vendored package still declares `electron: 43.3.0` as a devDependency *and* overrides it at postinstall with the fork. Task 7 never says to delete the postinstall hook, so the fork-fetch stays in the tree as a live install step that Task 12's "verify ... no patched Electron anywhere in the dependency chain" would then have to catch at the end.

Established by reading the manifest. What would overturn it: if `fetch-electron.sh` is a no-op on unrecognized platforms and exits 0 — but it is not copied, so `bash` fails on a missing file regardless, and `bash` itself is not guaranteed present.
findings.fix: Add an explicit Task 1 item: remove the `postinstall` hook from `browser/package.json` and pin the stock `electron` devDependency, recording it as the first intentional divergence from upstream.

findings.title: The two-slot shm design does not make tearing impossible, contrary to the constraint it is written to satisfy
findings.body:
The agwinterm plan states a hard requirement — "Frames must never tear. ... the design must make a torn read impossible, not unlikely" — and its Technical Details claim the two-slot scheme delivers it: "The producer owns one slot at a time and the renderer reads the other. ... A frame in flight is therefore never the frame being read."

That holds only if the consumer never falls more than one frame behind, and nothing in the design gives the producer any way to know whether it has. The producer runs free at Electron's paint rate; the consumer is driven by a control-pipe message that must be received, dispatched through `ControlServer`, and then memcpy an 8 MB 1920x1080 BGRA slot. Concretely: producer publishes seq=1 into slot 0 and sends the message; paints frame 2 into slot 1, publishes seq=2, sends; paints frame 3 and — with only two slots — begins writing slot 0 again. If agwinterm is only now servicing message 1, it copies slot 0 while frame 3 is being written into it. Torn read, and the acquire/release pair on `ready` does not prevent it because the barrier orders the *producer's* publish, not the *consumer's* copy.

What the scheme does guarantee is that a half-written slot is never *published*. That is a different property, and it is the one the Technical Details paragraph actually argues for ("a producer that dies mid-write leaves a half-written slot that is simply never published"). The stated requirement is stronger than what is designed.

The test list does not cover this. Task 3's tests are all argument validation (short view, bad stride, slot out of range, bad name); Task 4's are the `(id, seq)` cache and malformed args. There is no test in which the producer runs ahead of the consumer — the only case where the property under test can fail.

This is reasoned from the plan text, not from code, since the code does not exist yet. What would overturn it: a consumer-side acknowledgement I have missed in the design — but the plan explicitly says "no lock is shared across the process boundary", which rules out the usual mechanisms.
findings.fix: Give the consumer a way to signal the slot it is reading — an in-use word per slot the reader sets and clears, or more slots plus a released-sequence the producer must respect — and add a test where the producer publishes N frames faster than the consumer drains them.

findings.title: The napi build script hardcodes .dylib/.so and will not find the Windows artifact
findings.body:
`engine/packages/pixel-react/scripts/build-native.mjs:9` is `const library = process.platform === "darwin" ? "libpixel_node.dylib" : "libpixel_node.so";`, and line 14 does `fs.copyFileSync(source, destination)` unguarded. `pixel-node`'s manifest declares `crate-type = ["cdylib"]`, which on Windows produces `pixel_node.dll` — no `lib` prefix, different extension. The copy throws ENOENT.

This sits on the critical path for Task 6 ("confirm the napi module loads under Node v22 on Windows") and Task 8 (which needs a built engine), because `pixel-react`'s `build` script is `npm run build:native && tsc`, and `browser`'s `start` script runs `build:engine` first. Neither task mentions this file.

The fix is three lines. The objection is not its size — it is that the plan's Task 6 scopes the Windows work on `pixel-node` entirely to Rust (`SurfacePixels` variants, `draw_frame` match arms), so an executor working that checklist has no reason to look at the JS build script until the build breaks, which is exactly the class of stall that costs a long autonomous run.

Established by reading both files. Nothing would overturn it short of the script being replaced during vendoring, which no task proposes.
findings.fix: Add a Task 6 item covering `build-native.mjs`: platform-select `pixel_node.dll` on win32 and fail with a named path rather than a raw ENOENT.

findings.title: The portability measurement's scope excluded every layer where the port actually breaks
findings.body:
The goal asks whether the reference count is a proxy that fails. Within its own scope it does not fail — I reproduced it exactly. Per-file counts of `rustix::|std::os::unix|termios|libc::|/dev/tty` across `pixel-core/src/*.rs` give 64 for `terminal.rs`, 2 for `herdr.rs`, 2 for `ghostty.rs`, 0 for the other 19. I also checked the 24 files the count never reached — `src/` has 46 `.rs` files, not 22, because `engine/`, `scroll/`, `selection/`, `surfaces/` and `tree/` are subdirectories — and all 24 score zero on the same pattern. On the two dependencies the goal names specifically: `fontdue` is fine (fonts are `include_bytes!`-bundled at `paint.rs:775` and `menu.rs:356`, not loaded from a system font path), and `arboard` is fine (one guarded call site, `clipboard_image.rs:56`, `.ok()?`; `engine/Cargo.lock:27-32` already resolves it to `clipboard-win` on this platform). `rustix` itself builds on Windows — I read `rustix-1.1.4/Cargo.toml:61,238-243` and `src/lib.rs:265,289,301`, where `pipe`/`shm`/`termios` are `#[cfg(not(windows))]` behind a target that is explicitly supported. So `cfg`-gating the source, as Task 2 proposes, is sufficient for `pixel-core`.

The problem is what the measurement was pointed at. It counted Rust identifiers inside one crate, and the brief promotes that to "the port is: replace one module, port one, drop one, keep nineteen" — a claim about the whole port. Every blocker I found is outside the measured region: the tty-by-path daemon architecture lives in `cli/` and `browser/` TypeScript; the `/bin/sh` launcher is `cli/src/main.ts:109`; the `bash` postinstall is `browser/package.json:7`; the `.so` assumption is a `.mjs` build script; the missing cell metrics are a *host* gap, not a guest one. `throttle.rs` — one of the nineteen — is even 60% macOS-only under `cfg`, though it degrades to a no-op cleanly (`supported()` returns `false`) and is not a build problem.

Established: the counts, the file inventory, the three dependency checks. What follows is that the brief's confidence is calibrated to a measurement of the one layer that turned out to be the least risky, and the maintainer is being asked to fund the port on that number.

What would overturn this: it does not overturn the architectural bet itself, which I think survives — keeping `pixel-core` really does look cheaper than dropping it, and the chrome really is untouched. It overturns the *sufficiency* of the evidence offered for it.
findings.fix: Before Task 1, run the same disposition pass over `browser/`, `cli/`, `store/`, `terminals/` and the JS build scripts, and record the result next to the `pixel-core` table so the two halves of the port carry the same standard of evidence.

findings.title: The file-based bring-up path has a read/write race and a staleness hole at frame rate, and its claimed cache benefit is nil for a browser
findings.body:
Task 5 specifies "write it to a temp path" (singular) and "reuse ids across frames so agwinterm's content-signature cache behaves as designed". Reading the consumer, both halves are a problem at video rate.

`ControlServer.cs:451-460` computes `long sig = ContentSignature(path)` and transmits only if it differs from the last accepted signature for that id. `ContentSignature` (`ControlServer.cs:487-496`) is `LastWriteTimeUtc.Ticks ^ (Length << 1) ^ hash(path)` — it never reads the bytes. Two consecutive browser frames written to the same path whose PNGs happen to be the same length, within whatever timestamp granularity the filesystem actually delivers, produce the same signature and the new frame is silently dropped in favour of the cached one. There is no error and no counter that distinguishes it from a legitimately-unchanged frame.

Worse, phase 1 does `ContentSignature(path)` then `File.ReadAllBytes(path)` synchronously while the producer, running free at paint rate, is already writing frame N+1 to that same path. `ReadAllBytes` either hits a sharing violation — caught by the bare `catch { data = null; }` at line 458, which silently degrades to "place the cached image" — or returns a partially-written PNG that the renderer's async decoder then fails on. Task 5 has a bullet for "survive a frame whose file write fails"; it has none for the read side, and the plan never specifies a unique path per frame or an atomic rename.

Separately, the stated rationale is inverted. The content-signature cache exists to skip re-transmits of *unchanged* images. A browser frame differs every frame, so the cache never skips, and "reuse ids across frames so the cache behaves as designed" buys nothing — every frame pays a full stat, a full file read, a PNG encode upstream and an async PNG decode downstream (`ControlServer.cs:474` hardcodes `KittyFormat.Png`). That matters because Task 8's frame-budget measurement is "the case for the shm path", and the plan describes the file path as a reasonable bring-up floor rather than as something that may be too slow to demonstrate the milestone at all.

The cache mechanics and the `catch` are established from the code. The race and the timestamp collision are reasoned from it — I did not measure NTFS `LastWriteTime` update granularity or attempt a concurrent read, and I could not, since the producer does not exist yet.

What would overturn this: writing each frame to a unique path, or `File.Move`-ing into place atomically, closes both holes — but then the id-reuse cache genuinely never fires, since `hash(path)` is in the signature.
findings.fix: Specify unique-path-per-frame (or atomic rename) in Task 5, drop the id-reuse rationale, and add cleanup of the resulting file churn to the existing temp-file bullet.

findings.title: The brief and the agwinterm plan already describe different `image.frameshm` wire shapes, and the brief is the document the plan tells you to read first
findings.body:
The goal asks whether the contract between the repos is pinned. Two documents currently describe it and they do not agree.

The brief's transport diagram (`docs/design/00-port-brief.md:124`) shows `{"cmd":"image.frameshm","args":{"handle":..,"w":..,"h":..}}` — a **handle**, flat args, `w`/`h`. The agwinterm plan's Task 1 defines `{"images":[{"id":N,"name":"Local\\...","slot":N,"seq":N,"width":N,"height":N,"stride":N,"format":N,"row":N,"col":N,"cols":N,"rows":N}]}` — a **name**, an images array mirroring `image.frame`, and `width`/`height`. Different field names, different nesting, and a materially different mechanism: passing a `HANDLE` across processes needs `DuplicateHandle` against the target process; passing a `Local\` name needs neither. The agwinterm plan's design is the coherent one; the brief's is the stale one, and the Windows plan's own Overview instructs the reader to "Read it first — it records what was measured rather than assumed".

A second field is unpinned even in the good version: the agwinterm plan's Task 3 says "restrict accepted names to a fixed prefix in the `Local\` namespace" without ever stating the prefix, and the Windows plan's Task 10 says "create the named mapping" without one. Neither document contains the string a producer must actually use.

The Windows plan's Task 10 precondition — that `docs/specs/image-frameshm.md` exists — is the right instinct and mitigates most of this. But that spec is also where the agwinterm plan's Task 6 writes its throughput measurement, so the file exists and is authoritative from agwinterm Task 1 while remaining incomplete until agwinterm Task 6. "The spec file exists" is a weaker gate than it reads.

Established by reading both documents side by side.
findings.fix: Correct the brief's diagram to the `images[]`/`name` shape now, before either plan starts, and state the literal `Local\` prefix in the agwinterm plan's Task 1 so both sides code against the same string.

findings.title: Every mode negotiation and query reply pixel-core relies on crosses ConPTY's input translation, which agwinterm's own source documents as lossy
findings.body:
The brief treats the ConPTY boundary as lossy in one direction only — "ConPTY strips APC" — and calls the other direction solved: "Input arrives *through* the pty as ordinary VT sequences ... so it needs no side channel". The input direction is also a translation layer, not a byte pipe, and agwinterm's own code says so about a neighbouring case.

`native/agwinterm-core/src/emulator.rs:1052-1056` carries this comment about OSC 9;9: "*Crucially this is the cwd form that conhost/ConPTY passes THROUGH to the client (it swallows OSC 7), so under a pty-host it is the only way the live cwd reaches the terminal-side emulator.*" That is a documented instance of ConPTY dropping a sequence that is not APC, discovered the hard way in this codebase.

Everything agwinterm sends the child goes through that path: `src/Agwinterm.Win32/Program.Sessions.cs:290` is `public void Respond(string reply) { ...; _s.Write(...); } // query reply -> PTY`, the same `Write` that `SendMouse` uses. So the DECRQM replies pixel-core waits on (`\x1b[?1016;1$y`), the `CSI 16 t` cell-size report, and kitty-keyboard CSI-u reports are all synthesized host-side and pushed into the ConPTY input pipe for conhost to reinterpret before the child sees them.

I established the mechanism — that these all cross the translation layer, and that the layer is known to drop things here. I did **not** establish that any specific sequence fails; I could not, since running the port is what would show that. The plausibility argument cuts both ways: agwinterm 0.17.2 is in daily use, so basic SGR mouse evidently survives for ordinary apps. Kitty keyboard reports and `$y` DECRQM replies are far more exotic and are exactly what `pixel-core` depends on.

The reason this bears on the decision at all is placement: the earliest task that would expose it is Task 9, after the Task 8 milestone has been declared reached. A cheap check — send one DECRQM through a Debug agwinterm to a child in VT-input mode and see what arrives — costs an hour and de-risks Tasks 3 and 9 both.

What would overturn it: that check coming back clean.
findings.fix: Add a probe to Task 1's baseline: from a child under a Debug agwinterm with `ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_INPUT` set, record the exact bytes received for an SGR mouse report, a kitty-keyboard CSI-u report, and a DECRQM `$y` reply. Record it next to the `cargo check` baseline.

findings.title: pixel-node pulls openh264 with the `source` feature — an unverified C++ build on the Task 2 and Task 6 critical path
findings.body:
`engine/crates/pixel-node/Cargo.toml:26` is `openh264 = { version = "0.9.7", features = ["source"] }`. The `source` feature builds the vendored OpenH264 C/C++ sources through a build script rather than linking a prebuilt library. Task 6 scopes the Windows work on `pixel-node` entirely to Rust surface variants and `draw_frame` match arms and does not mention it; nor do `tree-sitter` (six grammars, all C) or `mp4`.

This also touches Task 2, whose stated deliverable is "`cargo check --workspace` is clean on Windows". `cargo check` still runs build scripts, so a build-script failure in `openh264-sys2` would make Task 2's gate unreachable for a reason that has nothing to do with the tty seam it is actually testing.

I want to be exact about what I did and did not do here: I read the manifest, which is established. I did **not** attempt the build — the review is read-only and I was asked not to run builds — so I do not know whether it compiles under the MSVC toolchain on this machine. I am reporting it because the plan's task decomposition assumes `pixel-node`'s Windows risk is entirely in the Rust it names, and there are three C/C++ dependencies it does not name. It may well build fine, in which case this costs nothing to have checked.

What would overturn it: `cargo check -p pixel-node` succeeding on this machine, which Task 1's baseline run would reveal anyway if its error list is recorded per-crate rather than only for `pixel-core`.
findings.fix: Have Task 1's baseline record `cargo check` results per crate, not just `pixel-core`, so a `pixel-node` build-script failure is visible before Task 2 depends on a clean workspace check.

findings.title: The engine runs in a detached daemon that opens the client's tty by path — a mechanism with no Windows analogue, and no task addresses it
findings.body:
Upstream is a daemon/client split, and the daemon reaches the user's terminal by opening a *path*. I traced the whole chain: `cli/src/main.ts:119` `ownTtyPath()` shells out to the unix `tty` command and keeps the result only if it `startsWith("/dev/")`; `main.ts:301-303` refuses to run without it (`"not running on a tty"`); the path is sent over a unix socket to the daemon, which at `browser/src/daemon.ts:96-106` rejects any open without a `tty` and passes it into `createSession`; `browser/src/session/session.tsx:315` hands it to `createRoot({ tty: this.ctx.tty, ... })`; and `pixel-core/src/terminal.rs:348-349` does `File::options().read(true).write(true).open(tty_path)`. Meanwhile `main.ts:155` spawns the daemon `{ detached: true, stdio: "ignore" }` — it has no console of its own by construction.

On Windows there is no path that names another process's ConPTY. `CONIN$`/`CONOUT$` resolve to the *calling* process's own console, and a detached process has none. `AttachConsole(pid)` is the only handle-across-processes mechanism, it is one-console-per-process, and it attaches to a console the caller does not own.

This is established. What follows from it is that Task 3's design is placed in the wrong process: it says "read from the console input handle" and "enable VT input with `SetConsoleMode`", which assumes the engine owns the user's console. In upstream's architecture the engine is the daemon and never does. The output side is accidentally immune — frames leave out-of-band via the control pipe addressed by `AGWINTERM_SESSION_ID`, so it does not need the tty — which is likely why this never surfaced during design. Input has no such escape: nothing in the 13 tasks proposes forwarding stdin from the CLI client to the daemon, hosting the engine in the foreground process instead, or duplicating a console handle across the boundary. An autonomous executor reaching Task 3 has to invent one of those architectures with no brief to work from.

What would overturn this: evidence that the port intends to abandon the daemon model and run the engine in the foreground CLI process (`createRoot({tty: null})` is a supported shape — `session.tsx:313` has a `!this.ctx.tty` branch). If that is the intent it is a large architectural decision that appears nowhere in the brief or the plan, and it needs to be a task.
findings.fix: Add a task before Task 3 that decides where the engine process lives on Windows and how console input reaches it — foreground-hosted engine, or client-forwards-stdin-over-IPC. Task 3's console work cannot be specified until that is settled.

findings.title: Task 8 cannot launch the browser: the only launcher is the CLI, which Task 11 ports three tasks later
findings.body:
Task 8's first checkbox is "launch Electron OSR". There is exactly one launcher in the tree and it is unported at that point.

`browser/package.json:9` — `"start": "... && exec node ../cli/dist/main.js"`. The CLI is the entry point. `cli/src/main.ts:109` builds the launch command as `return { command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", line], cwd: browserDir };` — every browser launch goes through `/bin/sh`, which does not exist on Windows. Before that, `main.ts:65-68` sets `ELECTRON_DEV_BIN` to `["electron"]` for every non-darwin platform, and `main.ts:83-86` does `fs.existsSync` on it and calls `fail()` if missing — on Windows the artifact is `electron.exe`, so it fails there first. `main.ts:105-108` also wraps arguments in POSIX single-quote escaping and appends `2>>'...'` shell redirection.

That work is Task 11 ("port `cli/src/` entry points: `main.ts`, ..."). So Task 8 — the milestone the goal names as the most valuable thing to get right — sits three tasks before the code that makes it possible. This is established from the two files; what follows is that an autonomous executor at Task 8 either stalls or silently pulls Task 11's work forward, which makes Task 11's later "tests pass" gate meaningless because the code will already be there under a different task's name.

What would overturn this: if Task 8 is meant to bypass the CLI and invoke `electron.exe browser/dist/main.js` by hand as throwaway scaffolding. The plan does not say that, and it would still need the daemon-vs-foreground question above answered first.
findings.fix: Move the `main.ts` launch path (electron binary resolution, spawn without `/bin/sh`) out of Task 11 and into a task before Task 8, leaving Task 11 with the registry/paths/`ssh`/`sandbox`/`upgrade` surface it also covers.

findings.title: Nothing supplies cell pixel metrics on Windows — both of pixel-core's mechanisms are unavailable against agwinterm
findings.body:
Cell size in pixels is what Tasks 5, 8 and 9 all compute against (Task 5: "cell-span computation from pixel size and cell metrics"; Task 9: "the pane's cell metrics, since an off-by-one cell is a wrong click target"). `pixel-core` has exactly two ways to learn it, and on Windows+agwinterm neither works.

`terminal.rs:869-889` `cell_size()`: first `self.size()?.cell_size()`, where `size()` at `terminal.rs:847-855` is `termios::tcgetwinsize` reading `ws_xpixel`/`ws_ypixel`. Windows' `GetConsoleScreenBufferInfo` has no pixel fields — there is no equivalent to report. Second, it writes `b"\x1b[16t"` (`terminal.rs:880`) and waits 300ms for a reply, setting `cell_query_unsupported` on timeout.

agwinterm answers neither. I read its full CSI dispatch at `native/agwinterm-core/src/emulator.rs:964-1045`: the arms are `H f A B C D G d J K X m r L M @ P S T q`, and everything else — including `t` — falls to `HostAction::Unhandled`. There is no XTWINOPS. I also grepped `src/Agwinterm.Pty/ControlServer.cs` for `cell_width`/`CellWidth`/`cell_height`/`CellHeight` and found nothing, so the control pipe does not expose it either, even though agwinterm computes `_cellW`/`_cellH` internally (`src/Agwinterm.App/MainWindow.xaml.cs:225-226`).

Established: both mechanisms are absent. What follows is that `cell_size()` returns `None` on this target, and every pixel↔cell conversion in Tasks 5/8/9 has no input. Note upstream's own herdr fixture (`pixel-core/src/herdr.rs:260`) carries `cell_width_px`/`cell_height_px` in its info payload — upstream solves this by asking the *terminal* over a side channel, which is precisely the mechanism agwinterm's control API does not offer yet.

What would overturn this: an agwinterm control verb or environment variable carrying cell metrics that I failed to find. I searched only for those four identifier spellings in `ControlServer.cs`.
findings.fix: Either add a cell-metrics field to an agwinterm control response (a third repo-crossing contract, so it belongs in the agwinterm plan next to `image.frameshm`), or add `CSI 16 t` to agwinterm's CSI dispatch. Pin it before Task 5, not during it.
